To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

co-located mobile game design is a design space that can leverage mobility to support social play by: 1) co-locating players in physical space, 2) extending game mechanics to support physical play, and 3) designing asymmetrically to support different player roles and information.

(1) mobile games can leverage the mobility of the device to support co-located play in public spaces, which (2) can be used to create a pocket magic circle that supports asymmetric design and (3) can leverage physical interactions and spatial context to extend the game beyond its formal system.
mobile devices can support social play in co-location by affording co-location, supporting physical interaction using the spatial context, and supporting asymmetric design with information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and collaborative aspects of co-located play in mobile contexts.
designing for social play, specifically in co-located contexts using mobile devices.
designing games for social play and the affordances of mobile devices in social contexts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mobile devices, co-location and social play are important factors for the game design of mobile games.
the use of mobile technology in co-located contexts affords a new set of game design problems, which can be addressed by a pocket magic circle.
the design of social play in co-location and mobile contexts should be considered as an extension to game design in general.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mobile devices and co-located mobile game play support social play through: co-located play, spatial play, asymmetric play, and the concept of a Pocket Magic Circle.
we have identified a number of ways in which mobile devices and co-located contexts contribute social play, and we have proposed a framework to support designers to leverage these properties.
we contribute to game design theory and practice by identifying how mobile, social, co-located elements can contribute to social play in game designs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mobile devices and co-located contexts can support social interactions in game design by providing a pocket magic circle for game design.
mobile contexts and co-location can be used to support social play and collaborative game design, and that the concept of a magic circle can be expanded to account for this.
the design space for co-located mobile game design can be extended by leveraging the properties of mobile contexts.
